source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612
finding: Most direct test of Prelec-style SP on LLM crowds. SP, majority vote and confidence weighting gave no reliable gain over a single sample. SP prompt: ask the model for its answer, then ask what percent of language models would say YES.
numbers: 5 models (Gemma-3-4B, GPT-oss-20B/120B, Qwen3-32B/235B); 4 binary sets: HLE 35 q, BoolQ 100, Com2Sense 100, Predict-the-Future 100; 50 samples per q-model (T=0.7 and 1.0); 375,000 responses.
quote: Polling is not a substitute for verification.
limits: Small question counts; only binary tasks; prediction prompt asks about language models, not a real peer population.
agent_relevance: Do not assume SP helps a same-model sample crowd. Test it on our own tasks before wiring it in.

source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612 (HLE table)
finding: On the hard HLE binary subset SP helped only for the largest Qwen model.
limits: N=35 means one question is about 2.9 points; differences are within noise.
agent_relevance: SP gains on hard questions are not stable across models.

source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612 (BoolQ table)
finding: On BoolQ SP was about equal to majority vote, sometimes slightly above, sometimes below.
numbers: T=1.0 accuracy, majority vs SP: GPT-oss-20B 79.9 vs 80.0; GPT-oss-120B 80.0 vs 82.0; Qwen3-32B 77.0 vs 75.9; Qwen3-235B 69.9 vs 72.1; Gemma-3-4B 61.0 vs 60.1. N=100.
limits: Within about 2 points; N=100.
agent_relevance: SP is roughly majority vote here, at double the prompt cost.

source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612 (Predict-the-Future table)
finding: On unknowable forecasting questions every method sat at chance, as it should.
numbers: Accuracy 45-54% for all methods and models; SP vs majority e.g. GPT-oss-120B 50.4 vs 45.4, GPT-oss-20B 47.7 vs 49.3. N=100.
limits: No signal to extract, so this is a sanity check, not evidence for or against SP.
agent_relevance: Aggregation cannot create knowledge that no member has.

source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612 (Com2Sense table)
finding: On Com2Sense, majority vote and SP both fell far BELOW the single-sample average for three of four models.
limits: Paired-item structure probably makes consistent wrong answers score below chance; the paper does not fully explain.
agent_relevance: Majority vote itself can hurt when errors are shared; SP only partly rescues it.

source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612 (why it fails)
finding: Authors explain failure by correlated errors. Models agree on wrong answers, temperature does not add independence, and self-reported confidence tracks consensus nearly as much as truth.
numbers: On MATH the top wrong answer was 65-87% of wrong responses; models converged on the same wrong answer on 53% of erring questions; plurality flipped in only 2.9% of cases between T=0.7 and T=1.0; random-string control (10,000 prompts) still showed above-chance agreement. Inverse-SP reached about 80% on HLE but chance elsewhere.
limits: Inverse-SP is described as a diagnostic, not a method.
agent_relevance: SP needs an informed minority that foresees the majority error. Same-model samples rarely supply that. Use different models or different tools as the crowd.

source: Ai, Pan, Simchi-Levi, Tambe, Xu (2025) Beyond Majority Voting: LLM Aggregation by Leveraging Higher-Order Information
finding: Proves and shows by simulation that plain SP is worse than majority vote for LLM agents. Proposes Inverse Surprising Popularity (ISP) and Optimal Weight (OW) instead.
numbers: Theorem 4.1: E[Adv_ISP] >= E[Adv_MV] >= E[Adv_SP]. Simulation N=4 agents, accuracies 0.6-0.9, K=2: MV 85.13, SP 79.94, ISP 91.37. K=4: MV 92.64, SP 90.52, ISP 94.94. K=10: MV 95.54, SP 94.40, ISP 96.81.
quote: LLM agents are generally more powerful, so the systematic biases that SP exploits in human settings are much less pronounced here.
limits: Simulation assumes a specific symmetric information model. Plain SP is not run on the real LLM datasets; only MV, OW, ISP are.
agent_relevance: Drop plain SP for same-family LLM crowds. If we use higher-order information, use the inverse form or accuracy weights.

source: Ai, Pan, Simchi-Levi, Tambe, Xu (2025) Beyond Majority Voting: LLM Aggregation by Leveraging Higher-Order Information (real LLM results)
finding: On real LLM ensembles ISP and OW beat majority vote by small but significant margins. ISP is mostly a fallback; OW-L and OW-I win more often.
numbers: 16 ensembles from GPT-4o/3.5, Qwen2.5-14B/3B, Llama3.1-8B/3.2-1B, Phi-4/mini. Four strong models: UltraFeedback MV 72.21 / ISP 73.26 / OW 73.66; MMLU MV 85.24 / ISP 85.78 / OW 85.78; ARMMAN MV 89.32 / ISP 90.01 / OW 90.37 (column order read from text extract). t-stats vs MV: 12.53, 23.39, 3.22 (p<0.001). ISP beat MV in 95.83% of ensembles; best method in only 12.5%. Gains 0.54 to 14.2 points.
limits: Gains are about 1 point for strong ensembles; larger for weak ones. Options were shuffled.
agent_relevance: Weighted voting by estimated accuracy is cheap and beats plain vote; try it before any meta-prediction scheme.

source: Ai, Pan, Simchi-Levi, Tambe, Xu (2025) Beyond Majority Voting: LLM Aggregation by Leveraging Higher-Order Information (eight-model and hard set)
finding: Larger gains with eight models and with weak models.
numbers: Eight-model table: MV UltraFeedback 70.23, MMLU 87.19, ARMMAN 84.40; ISP 71.18, 87.92, 84.79; OW-I 72.44, 88.64, 84.94. MMLU-hard: MV 17.23 vs OW-L 24.79; ISP about 18.7 (cell labels garbled in extract).
limits: ISP number on MMLU-hard is approximate.
agent_relevance: Hard items are where majority fails and weighting helps.

source: Goel et al. (2023) On the Truthfulness of Surprisingly Likely Responses of LLMs
finding: Single-model analogue of SP. Score each answer by P(answer | question) divided by P(answer | '?') and pick the highest ratio. Big gains on TruthfulQA for base models.
numbers: TruthfulQA (817 q) MaxPost to MaxRatio: GPT-2 S 0.42 to 0.51; GPT-2 XL 0.36 to 0.52; LLaMA-2 7B 0.34 to 0.58; 13B 0.43 to 0.59; 70B (4-bit) 0.37 to 0.58. Up to +24 points. COPA LLaMA-2 70B 0.88 to 0.88; StoryCloze 70B 0.77 to 0.85, GPT-2 S 0.58 to 0.67.
quote: We call a response r surprisingly likely, if the score is higher compared to other responses.
limits: Base models only, log-probabilities needed. Categories where 'I have no comment' is correct fell: LLaMA-2 7B Misinformation 0.75 to 0.08, Logical Falsehood 0.86 to 0.29. COPA/StoryCloze are two-choice.
agent_relevance: Cheap prior-correction idea: divide by a no-information prior to remove the answer a model says by habit. Needs logits.

source: Mytsyk, Zhang, Krishnamurthy (2026) Mitigating LLM sycophancy with RL-based fine-tuning: Bayesian Truth Serum approach
finding: Uses Bayesian Truth Serum (the ancestor of SP) as the reward in GRPO training to reduce sycophancy, with no labels.
numbers: G=64 samples per prompt, each gives answer plus predicted group frequency. SmolLM3-3B on 1,000 synthetic true/false items (800/100/100): flip rate under user pressure 23% to 4%; accuracy under pressure 80% to 93%. Cross-model: Llama-3.2-3B, Phi-3-mini, Qwen3-4B, Gemma-3-4B.
limits: One synthetic author-checked dataset; small models; more compute than baselines; asymptotic theory; transient sycophancy rise early; unanimous groups give zero gradient; negation relabeling loophole. About 100k of 315k chars read.
agent_relevance: Training is outside our no-training rule, but the mechanism (reward answers more common than the group predicted) supports using self-predicted frequency as a sycophancy probe at inference.

source: Mytsyk, Zhang, Krishnamurthy (2026) Mitigating LLM sycophancy with RL-based fine-tuning: Bayesian Truth Serum approach (ablation and theory)
finding: Dropping the prediction score removes the effect; prediction score alone helps less. Proof: coordinated symmetric answering cannot beat truthful reporting.
numbers: Truthful prediction optimal at alpha=1 for every G; sycophantic answer earns strictly lower expected reward in the large-group limit.
limits: Authors call the surprise-is-the-cause reading a conjecture from one dataset.
agent_relevance: The self-prediction step carries the signal, not the vote alone.

source: Luo and Liu (2019) Machine Truth Serum
finding: First ML ensemble use of the SP idea: learn when the majority is wrong and then pick the minority label (HMTS, DMTS).
numbers: 15 base classifiers; 6 binary and 6 multiclass sets. In high-disagreement splits HMTS fixed 48 of 149 on Spambase (+32.2%) and 8 of 51 on Breast Cancer (+15.7%). Ensemble table: German AdaBoost 74.0, RF 75.6, WeightedMaj 74.8, HMTS 77.2, DMTS 76.2; Breast cancer HMTS 96.13 vs RF 95.07 (DMTS 94.01); Waveform DMTS 85.60 vs RF 83.60.
limits: Prior is estimated by a learned model, not elicited; DMTS worse than baseline on Breast Cancer; gains concentrated in high-disagreement cases; one preprint.
agent_relevance: Pre-LLM proof that a learned is-the-majority-wrong detector can add accuracy. A verifier-style classifier is the same idea.

source: Luo and Liu (2019) Machine Truth Serum (journal version, not read)
finding: Journal version (Machine Learning 2022) of Machine Truth Serum; only title seen in a search snippet; page redirected to a login.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Same as preprint.

source: Shinitzky et al. (2022) Exploiting Meta-Cognitive Features for ML-Based One-Shot Group-Decision Aggregation
finding: Learns from meta-cognitive features (confidence, predicted support) to pick the right answer one-shot. The most important feature is the SP quantity itself (own answer's predicted vs actual support).
numbers: 2,490 human responses over 22 problems; 77 random subsets of 30 responses; average solver rate 28%. Success rate RCR-Agg 64%, ACR-Agg 55%; best rule-based baselines 62-64% in the text table; abstract claims +20% to +35% over standard rule-based methods. McNemar p<0.0014 (SP vs RCR-Agg).
limits: Human data, hard puzzles; the stated +20-35% depends on which baseline set is used. Figure 1 values for SP itself not in the text.
agent_relevance: Predicted support is an informative feature; a learned selector over such signals could be trained on our agent's logs.

source: Hosseini, Mandal, Shah, Shi (2021) Surprisingly Popular Voting Recovers Rankings, Surprisingly!
finding: Extends SP to ranking with partial votes and partial predictions; even a little prediction information helps over classical voting.
numbers: Mechanical Turk study with six elicitation formats (None/Top/Rank prediction x Top/Rank vote), three domains, 5 q per format per domain after tutorials; 82% passed quiz; 95% CIs; Kendall-tau distance to ground truth ranking compared with six conventional voting rules.
limits: Numeric Kendall-tau values are in figures, not text; human crowd, not LLM.
agent_relevance: Top-only prediction is a cheap format for a text agent: ask which option most voters will pick.

source: Trott (2024) Large Language Models and the Wisdom of Small Crowds
finding: GPT-4 matches a crowd of only 2-11 humans on word-rating tasks. No SP or meta-prediction was used; only plain averaging.
numbers: GPT-4 (T=0, gpt-4-0613) vs gold ratings: concreteness rho 0.80 vs human 0.67 (NNB 3); relatedness 0.80 vs 0.78 (NNB 2); valence 0.75 vs 0.55 (NNB 11 Spearman); iconicity 0.595 vs 0.37 (NNB 5-8).
limits: Subjective rating tasks, one model; NNB varies with task.
agent_relevance: One strong model is worth a small human crowd; any SP benefit must be judged against that.

source: Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd (2026) arXiv 2606.29661
finding: Ensemble strength comes from diversity across model families, not count. No SP used. GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Pro are nearly interchangeable.
numbers: 113 Metaculus binary questions (May-July 2025); five forecasters; budget of 5 samples: best was 2 FT-gpt-oss-120b, 1 each Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5, Grok 4; weights about 0.56/0.26/0.18; Grok 4 most irreplaceable (replaceability about 1.7 vs 0.6 for FT).
limits: Read through an alphaxiv summary page only; one forecasting set; log score.
agent_relevance: If we build a crowd for SP or voting, mix model families; same-family samples add little.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Search snippet only: 12-LLM ensemble forecast on 31 binary questions matched 925 human forecasters; simple median was a strong aggregator; giving LLMs the human median improved them. Not SP.
numbers: 12 LLMs vs 925 humans, 31 questions (from snippet)
limits: Not opened; numbers from search summary.
agent_relevance: Median or mean of diverse models is a strong baseline that SP must beat.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem
finding: Founding paper. Headline claim from a practitioner page in a search snippet: 21.3% fewer errors than majority vote and 24.2% fewer than confidence-weighted vote.
numbers: 21.3% and 24.2% error reduction (second-hand)
limits: Not opened this session; belongs to angles A and B.
agent_relevance: Defines the target our code test must reproduce.

source: Wikipedia (2026) Surprisingly popular
finding: Gives only a worked hypothetical (Philadelphia/Harrisburg): average right Yes 65 No 35; popular Yes 75 No 25; difference Yes -10, No +10, so No wins. Cites Prelec 2017 and Hosseini 2021.
limits: No study results or LLM mentions on the page.
agent_relevance: The rule in code: pick the option with the largest (actual share minus mean predicted share).

source: Ai, Pan, Simchi-Levi, Tambe, Xu (2025) Beyond Majority Voting: LLM Aggregation by Leveraging Higher-Order Information (formal rule)
finding: Formal form for LLMs: SP picks the answer maximising actual frequency minus average predicted frequency; ISP uses the counterfactual conditional prediction and assumes agents predict higher for answers matching their own.
numbers: Equations (3)-(4); a K=2 example where ISP is right with probability 1 while SP and MV are not.
limits: Assumes random option shuffling and symmetric information structure.
agent_relevance: Spec for a code test: needs P(A_i | A_j) tables estimated from the sample.

source: Generative Self-Aggregation (listing only)
finding: Snippet only: the LLM merges its own several responses into a new answer, claimed to improve quality without a discriminative judge. Alternative to vote-based selection.
limits: Not opened; no numbers read.
agent_relevance: Alternative to SP: have the model synthesise rather than vote.

source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612 (confidence weighting)
finding: Confidence-weighted voting also failed to beat majority reliably; on HLE it hurt Qwen models.
numbers: HLE: Qwen3-32B majority 25.1 vs conf-weighted 17.3; Qwen3-235B 20.2 vs 14.6; BoolQ GPT-oss-120B 80.0 vs 84.0 (a gain).
limits: Mixed sign by dataset.
agent_relevance: Verbalised confidence tracks agreement, so it carries little extra information.

source: Amiri-Margavi et al. (2025) Enhancing Answer Reliability Through Inter-Model Consensus
finding: Cross-model consensus among GPT-4, Claude-3-Opus, Gemini-1.5-Flash, LLaMA-3-70B on PhD-level statistics questions without ground truth. Consensus only; no SP.
numbers: Two or three models agreeing: Claude 100%, Gemini and GPT-4 98%, LLaMA 92%; reliability vs question-writer: Claude 92%, GPT-4 90%, Gemini 88%, LLaMA 77%.
limits: Agreement is not accuracy; no ground truth.
agent_relevance: Agreement among models is easy to get; a weak truth signal.

source: arXiv listing for 'surprisingly popular' (2026-11-01)
finding: Exact-phrase arXiv search returned 8 items; follow-ups: 2406.00870 and 2411.08367 (Hosseini, Mandal, Puhan), 2505.10377 Two-Round Voting, 2110.00952 Information Elicitation Meets Clustering, 2108.11173 SP in particle swarm optimisation. Only titles read.
numbers: 8 results; none about LLMs in the exact phrase
limits: Titles only; the two LLM-era SP studies (2510.01499, 2603.06612) were found through other searches.
agent_relevance: The LLM literature on SP is thin: two direct tests, both negative for plain SP.
